title: The Dioscuri and the Sons of Aphareus

summary.text: Leda's twins Castor and Polydeuces carried off the daughters of Leucippus and came to blows with their Messenian cousins Idas and Lynceus — over a stolen herd of cattle, or over the stolen brides themselves. Castor was killed and both sons of Aphareus perished; Polydeuces shared his immortality so that the brothers live on alternate days, and Tyndareus handed Sparta to Menelaus.
summary.citation: Apollod. 3.11.2; Hyg. Fab. 80; Ov. Fasti 5.699–720; Paus. 4.3.1; Hom. Od. 11.298–304

chapters.title: Cousins of Lacedaemon and Messenia
chapters.text: Leda bore Castor, tamer of horses, and Polydeuces the boxer. Homer makes both of them Tyndareus' sons, and Apollonius has them born at a single birth in his house; but Apollodorus says Zeus came to Leda as a swan on the same night as her husband, and with Hyginus he gives Polydeuces and Helen to the god, Castor and Clytemnestra to the king. Their cousins in Messenia were the sons of Aphareus, Tyndareus' brother through their mother Gorgophone: Idas, the strongest man then living, who raised his bow against Apollo himself for Marpessa, and Lynceus, who could see even what lay beneath the ground. The four hunted the Calydonian boar together and rowed in the Argo.

chapters.title: The daughters of Leucippus
chapters.text: Among the daughters of Leucippus were Hilaira and Phoebe. Apollodorus says the twins, wanting them for wives, carried them off from Messene and married them: Phoebe bore Mnesileus to Polydeuces, Hilaira bore Anogon to Castor. Hyginus makes the seizure a theft, for the girls were already promised to Idas and Lynceus, and Ovid too has each son of Aphareus pledged to Leucippus as a son-in-law. At Sparta Pausanias found a sanctuary of the sisters whose maiden priestesses were themselves called Leucippides, and noted that the poet of the Cypria made them daughters of Apollo.

chapters.title: Cattle from Arcadia
chapters.text: What set the cousins against each other is told two ways. In Apollodorus the four drove a herd out of Arcadia and left Idas to share it. He cut a cow into quarters and ruled that whoever finished his portion first should have half the booty, and the second the rest — then bolted his own portion and his brother's and drove the whole herd off to Messene. The Dioscuri marched on Messene, drove off that herd and much more besides, and lay in wait for the sons of Aphareus; Pausanias too makes the cattle the cause. Hyginus and Ovid tell of no raid: the Apharetids armed to win back their stolen brides, and each side, says Ovid, fought with equal right, love driving one pair to demand the girls and the other to refuse them.
chapters.citation: Apollod. 3.11.2; Paus. 4.3.1; Hyg. Fab. 80; Ov. Fasti 5.701–706

chapters.title: The deaths of the cousins
chapters.text: In Apollodorus, Lynceus' sharp eyes broke the ambush: he spied Castor in hiding and showed him to Idas, who killed him. Polydeuces brought Lynceus down with a cast of his spear, but as he chased Idas a stone struck his head and he fell senseless; then Zeus blasted Idas with a thunderbolt, as Pausanias also says, and took Polydeuces up to heaven. In Ovid it was Lynceus' sword that pierced Castor's chest, and Idas was stopped only by Jupiter's fire. In Hyginus Castor killed Lynceus; when he tried to keep Idas from raising a tomb for his brother, Idas ran him through, and Pollux then overcame Idas in single combat. Hyginus' star-book even sets Castor's death at Aphidnae, in a war of the Lacedaemonians against the Athenians.
chapters.citation: Apollod. 3.11.2; Paus. 4.3.1; Ov. Fasti 5.707–714; Hyg. Fab. 80, Astr. 2.22

chapters.title: Every other day
chapters.text: Carried up to heaven, Polydeuces would not take a deathless life while his brother lay dead, and Zeus let the pair pass one day among the gods and the next among mortals, turn and turn about — so Apollodorus tells it. In Hyginus, Jupiter had granted a star to Pollux alone, reckoning Castor a son of Tyndareus, until Pollux begged to share the gift; the Twins in the sky are the most loving of brothers, and Neptune gave them the power to save shipwrecked men. Ovid gives Pollux the plea that half the gift is worth more than the whole. Homer sets the alternation beneath the earth, which holds both alive: by Zeus' favour they live one day and are dead the next, with honour equal to the gods'.
chapters.citation: Apollod. 3.11.2; Hyg. Fab. 80, Astr. 2.22; Ov. Fasti 5.715–720; Hom. Od. 11.301–304

chapters.title: Sparta passes to Menelaus
chapters.text: With the Dioscuri gone to the gods, Tyndareus summoned Menelaus, Helen's husband, and handed the kingship of Sparta over to him. Messenia lost its royal line: with both sons of Aphareus dead his house had no male heir, and the kingdom passed to Nestor son of Neleus. The Spartans showed Castor's tomb with a sanctuary built over it — the sons of Tyndareus, they said, were not held to be gods until forty years after the fight — and a trophy Polydeuces raised over Lynceus. At Troy, Helen would search the Achaean ranks from the wall for her two brothers, not knowing that the earth already held them in their Lacedaemonian homeland.
